practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the characteristic of innovation?
A) Coming up with a completely new business idea
B) Turning a creative idea into a working product or process
C) Accepting the possibility that a business may fail
D) Explaining the benefits of a product to a potential customer
practice_questions.marks: B) Turning a creative idea into a working product or process [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one characteristic of a successful entrepreneur that involves persuading suppliers to offer better terms.
practice_questions.marks: Negotiation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'determination' as an entrepreneur characteristic.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks.

Acceptable content:
• Determination is the ability to keep working towards a goal despite setbacks or difficulties [1 mark]
• Extended: for example, continuing to improve a product after slow early sales rather than giving up [1 mark]

Do not accept generic phrases like 'working hard' without reference to persisting through difficulty.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the characteristic of communication helps an entrepreneur to run a successful start-up. Use the words 'because' or 'therefore' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks.
• Identifies that communication involves clearly explaining value to customers, staff or investors [1 mark]
• Explains the mechanism: because customers understand the product's benefits, they are more likely to buy [1 mark]
• States the consequence: therefore sales revenue increases, helping the business cover its costs and grow [1 mark]

Example answer: Communication means the entrepreneur can clearly explain their product to potential customers [1]. Because customers understand what makes the product worth buying, they are more likely to make a purchase [1]. Therefore, strong communication skills lead to higher sales revenue and a better chance of the business surviving its first year [1].

practice_questions.text:
Zara Okafor is starting a small sustainable clothing brand called 'Bramble & Thread' from her home in Sheffield. She has designed a range of upcycled-fabric jackets and wants to sell them at local markets and online. She has no previous business experience and has invested £3,000 of personal savings.

Analyse how two of the seven entrepreneur characteristics could help Zara build her business successfully.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (3 marks per characteristic).

Mastering (5–6 marks): Two characteristics are identified and fully analysed with specific reference to Zara's situation (upcycled fabric, local markets, online selling, no experience, £3,000 investment). Each point has a clear because-therefore chain and embeds scenario detail.

Secure (3–4 marks): Two characteristics identified and explained with some application to the scenario. At least one specific detail used meaningfully.

Developing (1–2 marks): One characteristic explained or two named without analytical development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable content (any two well-developed):
• Creativity: designing distinctive upcycled jackets gives Bramble & Thread a product that stands out at a market stall. Because customers are drawn to something they have not seen before, Zara can attract buyers away from mass-produced alternatives, helping her build an early customer base.
• Risk-taking: investing £3,000 of personal savings before she has any customers is a financial risk. Because she has committed this capital, she can afford materials and market pitch fees, which are necessary steps to generating any revenue at all.
• Communication: explaining the ethical sourcing and upcycling story to potential customers at market stalls builds trust and justifies a premium price. Therefore, strong communication helps Zara charge more and build loyalty.
• Determination: with no business experience, Zara will make mistakes. Determination means she analyses what went wrong rather than giving up, which increases her chances of survival past the first year.

practice_questions.text:
Kwame Asante set up 'Kopek Kitchen', a sole-trader home-baking business in Leicester, six months ago. He started with one product (Nigerian puff-puff doughnuts) and now stocks three local cafes and an online shop. He recently used his negotiation skills to reduce his ingredient supplier costs by 20%, and his confidence to pitch his products to a local food festival, which has offered him a prime weekend stall.

Discuss whether the personal characteristics of an entrepreneur are more important than having a good business idea when starting a new enterprise.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A balanced, well-developed discussion that uses both sides of the argument, embeds specific details from Kwame's scenario, and reaches a supported view. Arguments about characteristics and the idea are analysed rather than just listed. At least two scenario details (negotiation saving 20%, confidence in pitching, stocking three cafes) are woven into the analysis.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides discussed with some development. At least one scenario detail used meaningfully. A view is present.

Developing (2–4 marks): One side discussed or both sides mentioned at a surface level without analysis. Scenario details may be named but not embedded.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Generic observations with no reference to the scenario.

Content guidance:
For characteristics being more important: Kwame's negotiation cut costs by 20% (direct impact on profit); confidence allowed him to pitch successfully (direct impact on revenue growth); determination through the early months is what got him to three cafe stockists. A weaker entrepreneur with the same idea might not have persisted.
For the idea being crucial: without the distinctive product (Nigerian puff-puff), there would be nothing to pitch or negotiate about. Characteristics cannot substitute for a product customers want.
Conclusion: characteristics and idea work together, but for a start-up, characteristics often matter more in the short term because many good ideas fail due to poor execution — Kwame's case illustrates this.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a reward of starting a new business?
A) Increased hours of work compared to employment
B) Personal financial loss if the business fails
C) The independence to make your own business decisions
D) The stress of managing cash flow and suppliers
practice_questions.marks: C) The independence to make your own business decisions [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one drawback of risk-taking that is not financial.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any one of:
• Damage to health and wellbeing (stress, burnout, anxiety) [1 mark]
• Poor work-life balance (long hours, little personal time) [1 mark]
• Strain on personal relationships (pressure on family and friendships) [1 mark]

Do not accept 'financial loss' or 'losing money' for this question.

practice_questions.text: Describe one reward that motivates entrepreneurs to start a business, other than financial reward.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks.

Acceptable content (any one described):
• Independence: the entrepreneur is their own boss, free to make decisions about what to sell, how to work and who to hire [1 mark]. This means they are not answerable to a manager and can build a business that reflects their own values and vision [1 mark].
• Self-satisfaction: the pride and sense of achievement that comes from building a successful business from scratch [1 mark]. Seeing an idea become a product that customers value provides personal fulfilment that employment often cannot match [1 mark].
• Making a difference: the ability to create local jobs, supply products that benefit the community or run a business based on ethical principles [1 mark]. This social impact can be highly motivating, particularly for entrepreneurs whose goal is community benefit as much as profit [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how the drawback of poor work-life balance could affect an entrepreneur who has recently started a new business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks.

Mastering (4 marks): A fully developed because-therefore explanation that identifies the drawback accurately, explains the mechanism by which it arises for a new entrepreneur, and states the consequence for the entrepreneur's life and potentially for the business.

Secure (2-3 marks): The drawback is identified and explained with one development point, but the chain is incomplete.

Developing (1 mark): The drawback is named or a very basic description is given.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable content:
• A new entrepreneur often has more work than they can complete in a standard day, so evenings and weekends are spent on admin, marketing, stock management and bookkeeping [1].
• Because there is no one else to delegate to in a small start-up, the owner must do every task themselves [1].
• Therefore, the entrepreneur has little time for personal interests, exercise or rest [1].
• In the long run, this can lead to fatigue or burnout, which may in turn affect the quality of business decisions and increase the risk of business failure [1].

practice_questions.text:
Cassie Obi left a well-paid accounting job to launch 'Verd & Vine', a small organic herb farm and delivery box scheme near Shrewsbury. In her first year she worked 65 hours a week, reinvested all profit back into the farm, and rarely saw her young children during term-time evenings. She reports feeling deeply satisfied by what she has built, but admits the financial pressure and time away from family have been harder than she expected.

Discuss whether the rewards of running 'Verd & Vine' outweigh the drawbacks for Cassie.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A balanced, developed discussion that uses specific details from Cassie's scenario (65-hour weeks, reinvested profit, time away from children, self-satisfaction) to analyse both sides. Both rewards and drawbacks are explored with because-therefore chains. The conclusion goes beyond listing and gives a reasoned, supported view.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides discussed with some development. At least two scenario details embedded. A conclusion present.

Developing (2–4 marks): One side explored with some development, or both sides listed without analysis. Scenario details may be named but not analytically used.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Generic statements with no scenario reference.

Content guidance:
Rewards: self-satisfaction (explicitly stated by Cassie); independence (left a corporate job to build her own venture, set her own direction); potential for future financial reward as the farm grows; making a difference (organic food supply to local community).
Drawbacks: work-life balance (65 hours a week, minimal time with children); financial (no immediate income from profit reinvested); health and wellbeing risk as 65-hour weeks are unsustainable long-term; personal relationships (children affected by limited evening contact).
Conclusion: for Cassie, the satisfaction and independence appear to compensate for the current drawbacks, but the relationship with her children is a significant cost that cannot be reduced to money — this suggests the balance may tip depending on how long the current pressures last.

practice_questions.text:
Kweku Asante is considering leaving his job to start 'Bright Grounds', a speciality coffee roasting business in Newcastle. He has two young children and a mortgage, and has saved £12,000 to invest in the business. His partner works part-time.

Justify whether Kweku should start the business now or wait until he is in a stronger financial position.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-reasoned recommendation for one option, using specific details from Kweku's scenario (two children, mortgage, £12,000 savings, partner works part-time) to weigh the financial and personal drawbacks against the rewards of starting now. The conclusion is evaluative and goes beyond summarising prior points.

Secure (3–4 marks): A recommendation is made with reasonable analysis. At least one scenario detail used analytically. Some drawbacks and rewards weighed.

Developing (1–2 marks): A recommendation is present but with limited reasoning or only one side considered.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant recommendation or analysis.

Content guidance:
Case for starting now: market conditions may change; motivation is highest now; earlier start means earlier profitability; £12,000 may be sufficient for a home-roasting set-up with low overheads.
Case for waiting: mortgage and two children mean financial risk is very high — a financial drawback (losing £12,000) could have serious consequences for the whole family; partner's part-time income provides some cushion but not security; health/wellbeing and relationship drawbacks would compound an already stretched family situation.
Recommendation: waiting until savings are larger (or the mortgage is smaller) is the more justifiable choice given Kweku's specific financial commitments — the drawbacks outweigh the rewards at this particular moment in his personal circumstances.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of primary research?
A) Reading a Mintel report on the UK snack food market
B) Reviewing a competitor's pricing on their website
C) Conducting a consumer trial with 30 target customers
D) Looking at government statistics on household income
practice_questions.marks: C) Conducting a consumer trial with 30 target customers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name of one commercial secondary research provider that publishes market reports for start-up entrepreneurs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mintel [1 mark]

Also accept: any named market research organisation that publishes commercial industry reports.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage of using a focus group as a primary research method.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks.

Acceptable content:
• A focus group generates in-depth qualitative data by allowing participants to build on each other's responses [1 mark]
• This reveals opinions and motivations that a closed questionnaire would miss [1 mark]

Also accept: the group discussion can surface unexpected objections or ideas the entrepreneur had not considered; useful for testing product concepts or brand names before committing to them.

practice_questions.text: Explain why using 'the internet' as a market research method is not enough to earn marks in an exam answer. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks.
• States that the internet is not a stand-alone research method [1 mark]
• Explains that the method is the activity, not the platform [1 mark]
• Gives a specific example of a named method that can be conducted via the internet [1 mark]

Example answer: The internet is not a market research method — it is a platform through which methods can be conducted [1]. The named method is what matters, for example conducting an online questionnaire or accessing a Mintel report [1]. A student who writes 'use the internet' without naming the specific method (questionnaire, competitor data, government statistics) has not identified a method and will not earn the mark [1].

practice_questions.text:
Hana Nkosi is planning to launch 'Saffron & Seed', a small artisan candle business in York. She has a budget of £500 for market research and wants to find out whether local customers would pay a premium price for ethically sourced candles. She is choosing between distributing an online questionnaire to a local Facebook group or running a consumer trial by giving 20 sample candles to friends and family.

Analyse which market research method would be more useful for Hana.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A focused analytical response that evaluates both methods using specific details from Hana's situation (premium pricing question, ethical sourcing angle, £500 budget, local Facebook group, 20 sample candles). Each method is assessed for relevance, reliability and practicality in this specific context. A supported conclusion is present.

Secure (3–4 marks): Both methods are explained with some development. At least one scenario detail used analytically. A conclusion is present.

Developing (1–2 marks): One method described or both mentioned at a surface level. Little connection to the scenario.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Content guidance:
Online questionnaire: reaches a larger sample within a £500 budget; generates quantitative data about price sensitivity; limitation is that Facebook group members are self-selecting and may not represent the full target market.
Consumer trial: generates real behavioural data (do people actually like the product when they use it?) rather than reported intent; more directly relevant to the premium pricing question; limitation is the sample of 20 is small and friends/family may give biased positive feedback.
Conclusion: the consumer trial is arguably more useful for the specific question (willingness to pay for an ethical product) because real usage generates more honest data than stated intentions — but Hana should expand the sample beyond close contacts to reduce bias.

practice_questions.text:
Jamil Rahman is planning to open a specialist board game café in Southampton. He has gathered two types of data: a questionnaire completed by 120 local residents (which found that 68% would visit such a café) and a Mintel report on the UK board game market (which shows the sector has grown 35% in five years).

Discuss how useful each source of market research data is for Jamil's decision to proceed with opening the business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks.

Mastering (8–9 marks): A balanced discussion that analyses both sources, embeds specific data from the scenario (68%, 120 respondents, 35% sector growth, Mintel), evaluates reliability of each source, and reaches a supported conclusion about whether the combined evidence is sufficient to proceed.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both sources are discussed with development. Specific scenario details are used. A conclusion is present.

Developing (2–4 marks): One source analysed or both described at a surface level. Scenario details may be named but not embedded analytically.

Emerging (0–1 mark): Generic observations about research.

Content guidance:
Questionnaire: primary, so specific to Southampton; 68% is encouraging; limitation is that stated intent often overstates actual purchase behaviour, and 120 respondents in a city may not be a fully representative sample.
Mintel report: reliable industry-level data from a respected provider; 35% growth is a strong trend signal; limitation is it is national not local, so it may not reflect demand specifically in Southampton. Also may not be recent enough.
Conclusion: the combination of primary intent data and secondary trend data is stronger than either alone, but Jamil should consider a test marketing approach (e.g. a pop-up event) before committing to a full lease — real purchase data would be more reliable than questionnaire intent.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of lifestyle segmentation?
A) Targeting customers who live within five miles of the shop
B) Targeting customers who earn more than £40,000 per year
C) Targeting customers who prioritise ethical and sustainably made products
D) Targeting female customers aged 18 to 30
practice_questions.marks: C) Targeting customers who prioritise ethical and sustainably made products [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the six bases a business can use to segment its market.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct segmentation base, up to 2 marks.

Acceptable answers: age / gender / occupation / income / location / lifestyle.

Do not accept vague answers such as 'by type of customer' unless a specific base is identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'occupation' as a basis for market segmentation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks.
• Occupation segmentation groups customers according to their job type or professional role [1 mark]
• For example, a business selling specialist legal software targets solicitors and barristers rather than the general public [1 mark]

Also accept any example of a business product matching an occupational group.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit of market segmentation for a small start-up business. Use the words 'because' or 'therefore' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks.

Mastering (4 marks): A fully developed because-therefore explanation that identifies a specific benefit, explains the mechanism, and states the outcome for the start-up.

Secure (2-3 marks): The benefit is identified and explained with one development point, but the chain is incomplete.

Developing (1 mark): A benefit is named with no development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable content (any one benefit fully developed):
• Targeted marketing: because the start-up focuses its advertising on the specific segment most likely to buy, its limited marketing budget is spent more efficiently, therefore reducing wasted spend and increasing the return on every pound invested in promotion.
• Meeting specific customer needs: because the product is designed around a defined group rather than a general market, it fits that group's needs more precisely, therefore customers are more likely to buy and return.
• Increasing profits: because the start-up can pitch its product at a price the target segment is prepared to pay (e.g. a premium segment accepts premium pricing), therefore profit per unit is higher than a one-size-fits-all approach would achieve.

practice_questions.text:
Aiden Cole runs 'Forge & Flint', a small start-up making premium hand-forged kitchen knives in Sheffield. He currently advertises his products to all adults nationwide using social media posts. He is considering switching to a more targeted approach, segmenting his market by occupation (professional chefs and serious home cooks) and income (mid-to-high earners).

Analyse how using these two segmentation bases could improve the performance of Forge & Flint.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-developed analytical response that uses specific details from Aiden's scenario (premium knives, Sheffield, social media to all adults, professional chefs and serious home cooks, mid-to-high income) to explain how both segmentation bases would improve marketing efficiency and revenue. A because-therefore chain is present for each base, and at least one limitation is acknowledged.

Secure (3–4 marks): Both bases are analysed with some development. At least one scenario detail used meaningfully. A conclusion or limitation is present.

Developing (1–2 marks): One base described or both mentioned at a surface level.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Content guidance:
Occupation (professional chefs): Aiden's premium knives have features that professional chefs value (precision, durability, hand-forged quality). Because this group uses knives for hours every day, they will pay more for a superior tool; therefore focusing on this segment justifies Forge & Flint's premium price.
Income (mid-to-high earners): currently advertising to all adults means reaching many people who cannot afford or would not prioritise a premium knife. Switching to income-based targeting means every advertising pound reaches someone within the price-acceptable range, reducing wasted spend.
Conclusion: combined, the two bases create a much sharper target — a professional cook on a decent income — which should reduce marketing cost per conversion and support the premium positioning.

practice_questions.text:
Mei Zhang is planning to launch 'Verdant Threads', a start-up selling sustainable, naturally dyed children's clothing made from organic cotton. She is deciding whether to segment her market by age (targeting parents of children aged 0-5) or by lifestyle (targeting parents who prioritise environmental sustainability).

Justify which segmentation approach Mei should use for the launch of Verdant Threads.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-reasoned recommendation for one approach, using specific details from Mei's scenario (organic cotton, natural dye, sustainability angle, children aged 0-5) to explain why one basis is more appropriate. The conclusion adds evaluative thinking beyond summarising earlier points.

Secure (3–4 marks): A recommendation is made and supported with analysis. At least one scenario detail used. Some acknowledgement of the alternative.

Developing (1–2 marks): A recommendation is present but with limited reasoning.

Emerging (0 marks): No recommendation or relevant analysis.

Content guidance:
Age (parents of 0-5): wider addressable group; easier to identify (new parents are a clearly defined demographic); Facebook groups for parents are accessible and low-cost to target. Drawback: many parents in this group do not prioritise sustainability and would choose cheaper alternatives, so reaching them does not guarantee conversion.
Lifestyle (sustainability-focused parents): smaller but better-matched segment; these parents are actively looking for exactly what Verdant Threads offers; word of mouth within sustainability communities can be powerful; messaging can focus on the ethical story which is Verdant Threads' core differentiator. Drawback: the segment may be smaller, limiting initial volume.
Recommendation: lifestyle segmentation is the stronger choice for launch because the product's key differentiator — organic, sustainably dyed — only appeals to buyers who value that story. Age segmentation alone would waste budget reaching parents who will simply choose cheaper alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a fixed cost for a small start-up?
A) Raw materials used in production
B) Packaging for each unit sold
C) Wages paid to part-time hourly workers
D) Rent paid on workshop premises
practice_questions.marks: D) Rent paid on workshop premises [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State whether each of the following is a fixed cost or a variable cost: (i) salaries paid to full-time staff; (ii) wages paid to part-time workers by the hour.
practice_questions.marks:
(i) Fixed cost — salaries are a set monthly amount that does not change with output. [1 mark]
(ii) Variable cost — wages vary with the number of hours worked, which rises and falls with production. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Coppice Candle Co makes artisan soy candles in Bath. In November it sold 400 candles at £9.50 each. Fixed costs for the month were £1,100 (rent £700, insurance £200, loan interest £200). Variable costs were £2.80 per candle.

Calculate the profit or loss made by Coppice Candle Co in November. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Revenue: £9.50 × 400 = £3,800
Total variable costs: £2.80 × 400 = £1,120
Total costs: £1,100 + £1,120 = £2,220
Profit: £3,800 − £2,220 = £1,580
[3 marks: 1 mark for correct revenue (£3,800); 1 mark for correct total costs (£2,220); 1 mark for correct profit figure (£1,580). Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors if method is correct.]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a business owner might be surprised to find that the business is making a loss even though monthly revenue has increased.
practice_questions.marks: A business can make a loss even as revenue rises if total costs have grown faster than revenue. For example, if the owner has taken on new fixed costs such as renting larger premises or hiring additional permanent staff on salaries, these additional fixed costs will increase total costs regardless of output level. This means that even with higher revenue coming in, the gap between revenue and total costs may widen in the wrong direction, pushing the business into loss. [1 mark for identifying that costs may have risen; 1 mark for identifying a specific cost type or example; 1 mark for a developed chain explaining the revenue–cost relationship and how this leads to a loss.]

practice_questions.text:
Ironwild Pottery is a small partnership in Derby making hand-thrown bowls. Fixed costs are £1,400 per month. Variable costs are £4.50 per bowl. In May, the business received total revenue of £5,200 from sales of 400 bowls.

Analyse whether Ironwild Pottery's current cost and revenue structure gives it a healthy financial position.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Accurate calculation of profit (revenue £5,200; variable costs £1,800; total costs £3,200; profit £2,000) with well-developed analysis of what that profit means for the partnership's financial health. Considers the implications of fixed vs variable costs — for example, if sales fall, the fixed costs remain, quickly eroding or eliminating profit. Reaches a supported conclusion about the risks and strengths of the current structure.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correct or near-correct calculation with some analytical comment on the cost structure or profit margin. Applies to Ironwild's context but may not fully develop the implications of fixed costs remaining constant if output falls.

Developing (2 marks): Calculates revenue or costs but does not reach a profit figure, or identifies the cost classification without analysis.

Emerging (1 mark): States a relevant term or makes a basic arithmetic attempt with no developed analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Glassroot Jewellery is a sole trader in Bristol selling handmade silver earrings. The owner, Priya, borrowed £8,000 to buy equipment. She repays £350 per month, of which £80 is interest and £270 is repayment of the loan itself. She also pays £600 per month in salaries to one part-time assistant on a fixed contract, and pays hourly wages of £9.50 to two casual workers who each work an average of 20 hours per month.

Identify which of Priya's financial outgoings are business costs and calculate her total monthly fixed and variable costs from these figures.
practice_questions.marks:
Business costs identified correctly:
• Loan interest (£80) — this IS a cost [1 mark]
• Loan repayment (£270) — this is NOT a cost; it is a repayment of borrowed capital [1 mark for correctly excluding it]
• Salary (£600) — fixed cost [1 mark]
• Casual wages: 2 workers × 20 hours × £9.50 = £380 — variable cost [1 mark]

Total monthly fixed costs = £80 (interest) + £600 (salary) = £680
Total monthly variable costs = £380 (wages)
[Full marks for correctly excluding loan repayments, correctly classifying all three costs, and showing the wage calculation. Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors if classification method is correct.]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following statements best describes the break-even quantity?
A) The number of units a business sells in its first month of trading
B) The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs
C) The point at which the business starts to make a profit above its target
D) The maximum number of units a business can produce
practice_questions.marks: B) The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Pebble & Thread is a start-up making handmade greetings cards in Edinburgh. Fixed costs are £900 per month. Each card sells at £6.00. Variable cost per card is £1.50.

Using the formula below, calculate the break-even quantity for Pebble & Thread.

Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)
practice_questions.marks:
Bracket: £6.00 − £1.50 = £4.50
Break-even quantity: £900 ÷ £4.50 = 200 cards per month
[2 marks for correct final answer of 200 cards; 1 mark if bracket is correct (£4.50) but final answer is wrong due to arithmetic error.]

practice_questions.text:
Mossvale Ceramics is a small Ltd company making decorative tiles. Fixed costs are £2,700 per month. Each tile sells at £15.00 and variable costs are £6.00 per tile. Mossvale currently sells 350 tiles per month.

Using the formula below, calculate the break-even quantity and identify whether Mossvale is currently in the profit zone or the loss zone.

Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)
practice_questions.marks:
Bracket: £15.00 − £6.00 = £9.00
Break-even quantity: £2,700 ÷ £9.00 = 300 tiles per month
Mossvale sells 350 tiles, which is above 300, so it is in the profit zone.
[3 marks: 1 mark for correct bracket (£9.00); 1 mark for correct break-even quantity (300); 1 mark for correctly identifying profit zone with reference to actual vs break-even output. Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors.]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which a profitable business might still experience cash problems.
practice_questions.marks: A profitable business may face cash problems if its customers are allowed to delay payment. For example, if a business sells goods worth £3,000 but agrees that the customer has 60 days to pay, the £3,000 is counted as revenue (and contributes to profit), but no cash has actually arrived. This means the business must still pay its own suppliers and wages out of existing cash reserves — and if those reserves are insufficient, the business may be unable to meet its immediate financial obligations even though it is profitable on paper. [1 mark for identifying a relevant cause such as late payment, paying suppliers upfront, or high stock levels; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (revenue recorded but cash not received); 1 mark for a developed consequence showing how this threatens the business.]

practice_questions.text:
Ridgewick Candles is a sole trader in York. She currently sells 500 candles per month at £8.00 each. Variable costs are £3.00 per candle. Monthly fixed costs are £1,750.

Her landlord has told her that rent will rise by £350 per month from next month. Her selling price and variable costs will stay the same.

Analyse how the rent increase will affect Ridgewick Candles' financial position.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Calculates or clearly explains the impact on break-even quantity (new fixed costs = £2,100; bracket = £5.00; new break-even = 420 candles, up from original 350 candles at £1,750 ÷ £5.00). Demonstrates the impact on profit (profit falls from £750 [£4,000 revenue − £1,750 fixed costs − £1,500 variable costs] to £400 [£4,000 revenue − £2,100 fixed costs − £1,500 variable costs]). Shows awareness that if actual sales remain at 500, the business is still above break-even but with a smaller profit, and analyses the risk if sales were to fall. Conclusion is grounded in the specific scenario.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly identifies that higher fixed costs raise the break-even quantity and reduce profit. Uses some specific figures from the scenario. Development is present but may not fully analyse the impact on the profit zone.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies that more units must be sold or that profit will fall, without quantitative support or developed reasoning.

Emerging (1 mark): States that costs will rise with minimal development.

practice_questions.text:
'A business that is making a profit does not need to worry about running out of cash.'

Discuss whether you agree with this statement. Use the example of Copperoak Furniture, a small sole trader in Bristol that sells bespoke oak dining sets at £1,800 each, with customers paying 90 days after delivery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Develops a clear and balanced argument. Explains convincingly why profit and cash are different concepts using the scenario (revenue counted at point of sale; cash arrives 90 days later; meanwhile wages, materials and fixed costs must be paid from existing funds). Identifies specific causes of cash problems (late payment, paying suppliers upfront, high stock tied up in bespoke orders). Reaches a well-supported conclusion that the statement is largely incorrect, with a nuanced point — for example, that a highly profitable business with adequate reserves may be resilient enough to manage the 90-day gap, but a start-up with limited reserves is at significant risk.

Secure (5–7 marks): Clearly explains the cash-vs-profit distinction with reference to the scenario. Develops both sides (why profit matters; why cash is still at risk) with some development. Conclusion is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies that cash and profit are different and gives one reason why a profitable business might still run out of cash. Limited use of the scenario detail.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Agrees or disagrees with the statement with minimal justification. Little or no use of the scenario.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best explains why the four Ps of the marketing mix are described as 'interdependent'?
A) A business uses all four Ps at the same time in every campaign
B) Changing one P requires a rethink of the others to keep the overall offer consistent
C) Each P is managed by a different member of the team
D) The four Ps always cost the same to implement
practice_questions.marks: B) Changing one P requires a rethink of the others to keep the overall offer consistent [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the four Ps in the marketing mix and give one example of each for a small start-up bakery.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the four Ps, each with a relevant example applied to a bakery, for example:
• Product — the range of sourdough loaves and pastries on offer, including the quality of ingredients and packaging. [1 mark]
• Price — using psychological pricing (e.g. £2.99 per loaf) to attract value-conscious customers. [1 mark]
• Place — selling from a market stall on Saturdays and through a website for pre-orders. [1 mark]
• Promotion — posting photos of fresh-baked goods on social media each morning to attract local customers. [1 mark]
[2 marks for any two P names correctly identified, each with a relevant, applied bakery example.]

practice_questions.text: Outline how a start-up selling handmade jewellery might use the marketing mix to create a premium brand image.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Product: use high-quality materials and distinctive design, with attractive packaging that reflects the premium nature of the product. [1 mark]
• Price: set a high price (e.g. price skimming or premium pricing) to signal exclusivity and quality to target customers. [1 mark]
• Place: sell through own website and select craft fairs or independent boutiques rather than mass-market retailers, to maintain an exclusive feel. [1 mark]
• Promotion: use high-quality photography and targeted social media content to build a premium, aspirational brand identity. [1 mark]
[Full 2 marks for any two consistent Ps, each applied to the handmade jewellery context, with a clear link to premium brand image.]

practice_questions.text:
Hawser & Loom is a small private limited company in Whitby making handwoven wool scarves. Each scarf is priced at £85. The owner sells exclusively through the business's own website and at two specialist lifestyle stores. She is considering dropping the price to £45 to attract more customers.

Analyse how reducing the price might affect Hawser & Loom's marketing mix.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies at least two P-interactions clearly and with analytical chains. For example: the lower price conflicts with the premium product positioning (£85 signals quality and craftsmanship; dropping to £45 may cause customers to question whether the quality has declined). The place strategy (specialist stores) may no longer be appropriate if the brand is repositioned as a mid-range product — specialist stores typically require brands to maintain a premium image. Promotion may need to shift away from aspirational imagery towards value messaging. Demonstrates clear understanding that the Ps are interdependent and that a price change cannot be made in isolation. Reaches a supported conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one clear P-interaction with development and some application to Hawser & Loom. Analysis is present but may cover fewer Ps or lack full development.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies that reducing the price will affect other elements of the mix but the links are superficial or incomplete.

Emerging (1 mark): States that the price will fall with limited analysis of any knock-on effect.

practice_questions.text:
Crannock Provisions is a small sole trader in Truro run by its founder, Bea. Crannock makes artisan chilli sauces using locally sourced Cornish peppers. Bea currently sells her sauces at £6.50 a bottle, which is higher than most supermarket alternatives. She distributes through two local farm shops and her own Instagram page. Sales have been slow and Bea is considering whether to change her marketing mix.

Evaluate whether Crannock Provisions should reduce its price to £3.99 as a way of improving sales.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Evaluates both the potential benefits and the risks of the price reduction, with clear and specific reference to the scenario. Benefits: a lower price may attract price-sensitive customers who have not bought at £6.50; it could increase volume and help cover fixed costs; it may widen the target market beyond premium buyers. Risks: £3.99 is close to mass-market supermarket prices, which could undermine the artisan positioning (locally sourced Cornish peppers, farm shop distribution) that justifies a premium price; it may force a rethink of place (farm shops may not stock a £3.99 product alongside artisan goods) and promotion (Instagram content built around premium craft food); and it may not increase profit if margins are already thin at £6.50. Evaluative conclusion adds new thinking — for example, that Bea should first investigate whether her current customers are price-sensitive or value-driven, and consider improving promotion before cutting price, because the limited sales may reflect a reach problem rather than a price problem.

Secure (5–7 marks): Discusses both sides with some reference to the scenario and some integration of P-links. Conclusion is present but may repeat earlier points.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies advantages or disadvantages of reducing the price without full integration of the marketing mix. Limited scenario application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): States a preference with minimal justification. Little engagement with the specific scenario.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a new start-up selling eco-friendly cleaning products might choose penetration pricing rather than price skimming when it first enters the market.
practice_questions.marks: Penetration pricing involves launching at a low price to attract customers quickly and build market share. This suits a new eco-friendly cleaning product because the market is competitive — there are already many established brands — so a high skimming price would deter customers who do not yet know the product and have no reason to pay a premium. By entering at a low price, the start-up can encourage trial purchases, build a customer base, and generate word-of-mouth recommendation. Once customers are loyal and familiar with the product's quality, the price can be raised. Price skimming, by contrast, works best for genuinely innovative or unique products with no competition — which does not describe a market with many existing eco-cleaning brands. [1 mark per developed point up to 4 marks: (1) what penetration pricing is; (2) why competition makes a high launch price risky; (3) how a low price encourages trial and builds market share; (4) why skimming would be inappropriate in this context.]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a third-party-generated social media post?
A) A business posting a photo of its new product on its own Instagram account
B) A business sending an SMS discount code to its mailing list
C) A customer sharing a positive review of a product on their personal blog
D) A business publishing a press release on its own website
practice_questions.marks: C) A customer sharing a positive review of a product on their personal blog [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage of using a press release as a PR method for a small start-up.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: it generates media coverage at no direct cost to the business; it is perceived as more credible than paid advertising because it comes from a neutral media source; it can reach a wide audience if picked up by local newspapers, radio or online publications. [1 mark for any one relevant advantage stated clearly.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two digital advertising mediums that a start-up selling eco-friendly stationery might use to reach customers.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of the following, each with enough description to show understanding:
• Social media (business-generated posts) — posting images of the product on platforms such as Instagram, with content reflecting the eco-friendly values of the brand to attract environmentally conscious customers. [1 mark]
• Podcasts (sponsorship) — sponsoring a podcast focused on sustainable living to reach listeners who already care about eco-friendly choices. [1 mark]
• Vlogs — creating video content demonstrating how the stationery is made from recycled materials, published on YouTube, to build brand authenticity and reach. [1 mark]
• Online banners — targeted display adverts shown to users who have searched for eco-friendly products. [1 mark]
[2 marks for any two named digital mediums with relevant description applied to the stationery context.]

practice_questions.text:
Yarrow & Stem is a small Ltd company in Hereford run by two founders, selling wildflower seed packets. They want to boost sales quickly before the spring planting season and have a promotional budget of £400. They are considering either a BOGOF offer or a local radio advertising campaign.

Justify which promotional option you would recommend to Yarrow & Stem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and developed with specific reference to the scenario (seasonal urgency, £400 budget, wildflower seed packets, small Ltd). The recommended option's advantages are explained with good reason chains, and at least one drawback of the recommended option or advantage of the alternative is acknowledged. The justification is grounded in the specific context — for example, BOGOF directly incentivises immediate purchase (important before spring), costs no cash outlay beyond reduced margin, and is easy to implement on a £400 budget; alternatively, radio can reach a local audience quickly and generate awareness beyond existing customers, but £400 may be insufficient for a campaign with meaningful reach. A developed conclusion adds a new evaluative point — for example, that BOGOF is the better choice because Yarrow & Stem needs to sell existing stock quickly rather than build long-term awareness.

Secure (3–4 marks): A clear recommendation with developed reasoning that uses some scenario detail. At least one reason chain is clear. Some acknowledgement of trade-offs.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with basic reasoning. Limited engagement with the specific scenario.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with little or no supporting reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Greybridge Brew Co is a small partnership in Sheffield producing craft coffee. The founders, Marcus and Amara, are deciding between two promotional approaches:

Option A: Invest £600 in a TV advert on a regional channel to reach a broad local audience.
Option B: Invite a popular local food blogger with 18,000 followers to try the coffee and write a review.

Analyse how each option might help Greybridge Brew Co achieve its promotional objectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Analyses both options with clear analytical chains and specific reference to the scenario. For Option A (TV advert): strong visual impact and broad reach, but expensive for a small partnership (£600 may buy limited airtime on regional TV); the advert is controlled by the business but is obviously promotional, which may not build the same trust as editorial coverage. For Option B (blogger review): a third-party-generated post that is perceived as independent and trustworthy by the blogger's 18,000 followers; it may cost nothing or a very small fee (product sample), meaning more of the promotional budget is preserved; however, the business cannot control what the blogger writes and a neutral or negative review could damage reputation. Explores the trade-offs explicitly and reaches a supported analytical conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one advantage of each option with some analytical development. Some reference to the scenario.

Developing (2 marks): Describes the two options without clear analytical chains or scenario engagement.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one or both options with minimal analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Bluebell Bath Co is a sole trader in Norwich making luxury bath products. The owner, Faye, wants to build a loyal customer base and is considering introducing a loyalty scheme.

Discuss whether a loyalty scheme is likely to be the most effective sales promotion technique for Bluebell Bath Co.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Develops both sides of the argument with clear reasoning and specific application to the scenario (luxury bath products, sole trader, building a loyal customer base). In favour: a loyalty scheme rewards repeat purchase directly, which aligns with Faye's objective of building a loyal base; it encourages customers to return rather than switching to a competitor for a lower-priced alternative; for a small business, knowing customers will return provides a more stable revenue base. Against: a loyalty scheme alone does not attract new customers — if awareness is low, there is nobody to retain; the administrative cost of running a points or stamp scheme may be significant for a sole trader with no support staff; other techniques such as a BOGOF on a bestselling product or a competition on social media might generate more immediate buzz and new customer acquisition. Evaluative conclusion adds new thinking — for example, that loyalty schemes work best once a customer base already exists, so Faye should focus first on advertising or PR to attract new customers, then introduce a loyalty scheme to retain them.

Secure (5–7 marks): Addresses both sides with some development and scenario reference. Conclusion is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies advantages or disadvantages of a loyalty scheme with limited balance or scenario application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): States a view with little justification or scenario engagement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a digital selling channel?
A) A market stall at a town centre
B) A face-to-face appointment at a customer's home
C) A listing on a social media marketplace
D) A pop-up shop in a shopping centre
practice_questions.marks: C) A listing on a social media marketplace [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two extension strategies a business could use to slow the decline of a product.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any two of the following (1 mark for the first correct answer — question is 1 mark; accept any single correct extension strategy):
• Increased advertising
• Price reduction
• Adding value (e.g. extra features, longer warranty)
• New packaging
• Entering new markets / geographic expansion
[1 mark for any one clearly stated extension strategy]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to sales and profit during the maturity stage of the product lifecycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct point, up to 2 marks:
• Sales have peaked and are stable (or: sales are at their highest level) [1 mark]
• Profit is typically at its maximum, but competition is intense and profit per unit may start to fall [1 mark]
[Both points required for 2 marks; 1 mark if only one is given]

practice_questions.text:
Greystone Press is a small independent publisher based in Sheffield, run by two partners. It sells illustrated books for children. The business is considering adding a digital channel to complement its current face-to-face sales at craft fairs.

Explain one benefit to Greystone Press of selling its books through an e-commerce website.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a point, development and contextual link:
• An e-commerce website would allow Greystone Press to sell books 24 hours a day to customers anywhere in the UK (1 mark), so it is not limited to the visitors who attend the craft fairs it currently relies on (1 mark), meaning revenue is not restricted to fair opening hours and the business could reach families across the country who would never visit Sheffield in person (1 mark).
[1 mark for a valid benefit; 1 mark for development; 1 mark for a contextual link to Greystone Press, craft fairs, or the illustrated children’s book market]

practice_questions.text:
Bramble & Slate is a small homeware brand run by founder Nadia from her workshop in Bath. She sells hand-thrown pottery mugs. Sales data over four years is shown below:
Year 1: 400 units sold | Year 2: 1,800 units sold | Year 3: 3,200 units sold | Year 4: 3,100 units sold

Analyse how the stage of the product lifecycle that Bramble & Slate is currently in might affect Nadia's marketing decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Student correctly identifies maturity from the sales data (rising steeply, now plateauing) and makes two or more developed analytical points linking the stage to specific marketing decisions. Uses contextual details (pottery mugs, hand-thrown, Nadia, Bath workshop) throughout. Analysis shows awareness that competition is intensifying and that Nadia must defend market share through promotion or differentiation rather than relying on novelty.

Secure (3-4 marks): Correctly identifies maturity or late growth and links the lifecycle stage to at least one marketing decision with some development. Some use of context from the scenario.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies a lifecycle stage (possibly incorrectly as growth) and makes a basic point about marketing. Little or no use of the scenario details.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic recall of the product lifecycle or a generic marketing statement with no analytical development.

practice_questions.text:
Bramble & Slate's sales have begun to slow. Nadia is deciding between two extension strategies:
Option A: Spend £2,000 on a social media advertising campaign targeting new customers aged 25-40.
Option B: Launch a new gift-set packaging range, selling the existing mugs in pairs with a gift box, at a higher price point.

Justify which option you would recommend to Nadia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified using specific contextual details (hand-thrown pottery, £2,000 budget, gift market, Bath workshop). The student develops a case for the chosen option, addresses a key drawback and explains why the drawback is manageable. The conclusion adds evaluative thinking rather than restating earlier points.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with developed reasoning using some contextual detail. One drawback of the chosen option is acknowledged.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning, but analysis is general and context is used only superficially.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes price skimming?
A) Setting a price in line with competitors to avoid losing customers on price
B) Launching at a low price to win market share quickly, then raising it later
C) Launching at a high price to earn maximum revenue from early adopters, then reducing it
D) Pricing just below a round number to make the product feel cheaper
practice_questions.marks: C) Launching at a high price to earn maximum revenue from early adopters, then reducing it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two factors that might influence the price a new business charges for its product.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any two of the following (1 mark for one correct answer on a 1-mark Identify question — if the instruction calls for two, treat this as a 2-mark response and award 1 mark each):
• Income levels of target customers
• Competitor prices
• Cost of production
• Stage of the product lifecycle
[1 mark for one correctly identified factor]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between penetration pricing and price skimming.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each accurately described strategy, up to 2 marks:
• Penetration pricing sets a low price at launch to win customers quickly, with the intention of raising the price later [1 mark]
• Price skimming sets a high price at launch to maximise revenue from early adopters, then reduces it as competition enters [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Hartwell Audio is a small start-up in Bristol that has developed a wireless speaker with genuinely new sound technology. There are no direct competitors at launch. Its target customers are music enthusiasts aged 25-45 with mid-to-high incomes.

Explain one pricing strategy that would be appropriate for Hartwell Audio at the launch stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Full marks for one fully developed point:
• Price skimming would be appropriate for Hartwell Audio (1 mark) because the product has genuinely new technology with no direct competition at launch (1 mark), which means early adopters who want to be first will pay a premium price (1 mark), allowing Hartwell Audio to earn high revenue in the early stage before competitors enter and force a price reduction (1 mark).
[Accept penetration pricing as a valid alternative with a developed and logical reason chain — e.g. that winning early market share quickly builds brand recognition before competitors arrive; award up to 4 marks for a well-developed and logically consistent chain.]

practice_questions.text:
Copper & Croft is a small sustainable homeware brand based in Edinburgh, run by founder Jess. She sells hand-stitched linen napkins. Her production costs are low, her target customers are mid-income households, and she is entering a market where several established brands already trade at similar quality levels.

Analyse which pricing strategy would be most appropriate for Copper & Croft.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Student identifies a specific strategy and develops two or more analytical points connecting all relevant contextual factors (mid-income customers, existing competition, low production cost, homeware market). The response shows awareness of trade-offs and reaches a supported conclusion about which strategy fits best and why the others would be less appropriate.

Secure (3-4 marks): One strategy is recommended with developed reasoning and at least one contextual link. Some reference to the competitive environment or customer income level.

Developing (2 marks): A strategy is named with a brief and mostly correct explanation, but the link to the specific business context is limited or absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A pricing strategy is named with a very brief or partially incorrect description.

practice_questions.text:
Vanta Coffee Co. is a new independent coffee brand launched in Manchester by founder Rahul. He is targeting busy office workers who currently buy coffee from large chain cafes. His coffee is of comparable quality to the established chains but his costs are lower.

Rahul is deciding between two pricing strategies:
Option A: Penetration pricing — launch at a noticeably lower price than the chains to attract customers quickly.
Option B: Competitive pricing — match the chains' prices and compete on quality and service.

Justify which pricing strategy you would recommend to Rahul.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified using specific contextual details (office workers, comparable quality, lower costs, large-chain competition). The student develops the reasons for the chosen strategy, addresses a key drawback and explains why it does not override the recommendation in this context. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with clear reasoning and some use of context. At least one drawback is acknowledged.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning but context is used only superficially. Analysis is limited.

Emerging (1 mark): A strategy is named with little or no reasoned justification.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following business structures gives its owners limited liability?
A) Sole trader
B) Standard partnership
C) Private limited company (Ltd)
D) A business with one owner and no formal registration
practice_questions.marks: C) Private limited company (Ltd) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct disadvantage, up to 2 marks:
• Unlimited liability — personal assets (home, savings) can be seized if the business cannot pay its debts [1 mark]
• Difficult to raise large amounts of finance, as banks see sole traders as higher risk [1 mark]
• The business depends entirely on the owner — illness or absence can stop it functioning [1 mark]
• All decisions rest with one person — no one to share workload or complementary skills [1 mark]
[Any two of the above for 2 marks; no further development required for Describe questions at 1 mark per point]

practice_questions.text: Outline one difference between a standard partnership and a limited liability partnership (LLP).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a point with development:
• In a standard partnership, all partners have unlimited liability and personal assets can be claimed to pay business debts (1 mark); in an LLP, members have limited liability, so personal assets are protected if the business cannot pay what it owes (1 mark).
[1 mark for identifying the liability difference; 2 marks for explaining the implication for personal assets]

practice_questions.text:
Perch & Frame is a small picture-framing business in Brighton run by Yasmin. She currently operates as a sole trader. A friend has offered to invest £15,000 in exchange for a 30% share of the business. Yasmin is worried about personal financial risk as the business grows.

Explain two reasons why Yasmin might consider forming a private limited company.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per point (statement plus development), maximum 4 marks:
• Limited liability would protect Yasmin's personal assets (1 mark) — as a shareholder in an Ltd, she could only lose her investment if Perch & Frame failed, meaning her home and savings would be safe, which directly addresses her concern about personal financial risk as the business grows (1 mark).
• Bringing in the investor as a shareholder creates a formal legal arrangement (1 mark) — it clearly defines the investor's 30% ownership stake and Yasmin's 70% majority, giving both parties legal clarity and preventing future disputes about control or profit sharing (1 mark).
[Credit any two valid, developed reasons linked to the scenario]

practice_questions.text:
Sable & Fern is a new zero-waste cleaning products brand founded by two friends, Priya and Joel, in Manchester. They are deciding how to fund the first production run.

Priya wants to use a crowdfunding platform. Joel wants to apply for a business grant.

Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of each funding option for Sable & Fern.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Both crowdfunding and grants are analysed with developed points on at least one benefit and one drawback of each. Contextual details (zero-waste brand, two founders, first production run) are embedded throughout rather than added as a label. The response shows analytical connections between the funding type and the specific situation Sable & Fern faces.

Secure (3-4 marks): Both options are addressed with some analytical development. At least one benefit and one drawback across the two options are developed. Some use of context.

Developing (2 marks): One or both options are described with limited analytical development. Context from the scenario is largely absent.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic and partly correct description of one funding option with no analytical development.

practice_questions.text:
Remy has decided to start a business. He is considering two options:
Option A: Set up as a sole trader selling handmade candles online.
Option B: Buy a cleaning franchise with an established UK brand.

Justify which option you would recommend for Remy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified with developed reasoning addressing the key trade-offs between control and risk (sole trader: full independence, unlimited liability, no proven model; franchise: lower risk, proven brand, but ongoing royalty costs and loss of independence). The recommendation is consistent and the conclusion adds a new evaluative point not already made in the body.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with clear reasoning and some awareness of trade-offs. The response is more developed than a simple list of pros and cons.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with brief and partly developed reasoning. Trade-offs are described but not fully analysed.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoned justification.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of a Chamber of Commerce?
A) A government body that issues grants directly to new businesses
B) A membership organisation that supports local businesses through networking and training
C) A bank that provides loans and financial advice to small start-ups
D) A legal firm that drafts contracts for new businesses
practice_questions.marks: B) A membership organisation that supports local businesses through networking and training [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which an accountant can support a new start-up business.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any one of the following (1 mark for one correct answer on a 1-mark State question):
• Setting up bookkeeping systems to track income and expenses
• Preparing tax returns and ensuring the business meets its legal tax obligations
• Advising on whether the business is generating profit
• Helping manage payroll for any employees
[1 mark for any one correctly stated function of an accountant]

practice_questions.text: Describe one way a local council enterprise department can support a new business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for a valid way and 1 mark for development:
• A local council enterprise department can help a new business find suitable premises in the area (1 mark) by providing information about available commercial spaces and local business rates, which reduces the time and cost the entrepreneur would spend searching independently (1 mark).
[Accept any valid function — local grants, local networking introductions, business rates advice — with a brief development of why it helps]

practice_questions.text:
Tansy is a recent graduate who has just launched a sustainable clothing brand from her home in Leicester. She has a strong product but no industry contacts, very limited business experience, and she needs funding to order her first large batch of stock.

Explain why a business angel might be a more suitable source of support for Tansy than a bank loan.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed reason chain:
• A business angel provides capital like a bank loan but also offers mentoring and industry contacts (1 mark), which is particularly valuable for Tansy because her main weakness is limited business experience and no contacts in the fashion industry (1 mark). A bank would provide the funding but would not offer the guidance Tansy needs to avoid common start-up mistakes (1 mark), meaning the business angel addresses both of Tansy's gaps simultaneously, though at the cost of giving up a share of ownership (1 mark).
[1 mark for identifying that a business angel offers more than money; 1 mark for linking the mentoring/contacts to Tansy's specific situation; 1 mark for contrast with a bank's limitations; 1 mark for awareness of the trade-off (loss of ownership)]

practice_questions.text:
Coppice Brew Co. is a new craft beer brand founded by two friends, Eli and Nadia, in a rural part of Wales. They have a product they are proud of, a small amount of personal savings, and limited knowledge of financial management or legal contracts. They are also struggling to find customers beyond their local village.

Analyse two sources of support that would be most appropriate for Coppice Brew Co. at this stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two sources of support are identified and each is analytically developed, connecting the specific benefits of that support to the specific challenges Coppice Brew Co. faces (limited finance, no financial management knowledge, no legal experience, limited customer reach). Contextual details (rural Wales, craft beer, two founders) are embedded rather than added as a label. The response shows awareness of why each source is more appropriate than alternatives.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two sources are identified with some development and at least one contextual link. The response shows understanding of what each source provides and why it is relevant.

Developing (2 marks): One or two sources are named with limited analytical development. The link to the specific business is weak or absent.

Emerging (1 mark): One source is named with little or no development.

practice_questions.text:
Iris is planning to open a children's art studio in a market town. She has found a good premises but is unsure whether to use a solicitor to draft her lease agreement or to sign the landlord's standard contract without legal advice, saving approximately £500.

Justify whether Iris should use a solicitor to review her lease agreement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified with developed reasoning linked to the specific context (art studio, market town premises, lease agreement, £500 saving). The student builds a reason chain explaining the risk of not using a solicitor and why that risk outweighs the cost, or develops a credible alternative if recommending against. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point rather than restating earlier arguments.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with clear reasoning and some contextual reference. At least one developed point about the risk or benefit of using a solicitor.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning but the analysis is general. Context is used superficially.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoning.
